findings.title: Options-object form enables `rejectOnClear` by default
findings.cause: The options destructuring at `index.js:6-7` uses `rejectOnClear = true`, so omitting the property flips the documented default from `false` to `true` whenever callers use `pLimit({concurrency: ...})`.
findings.impact: Code that migrates from `pLimit(1)` to `pLimit({concurrency: 1})` changes `clearQueue()` semantics from silent discard to `AbortError` rejection. Awaited queues can start failing unexpectedly, and callers that do not handle the rejection can surface unhandled rejections.
findings.evidence: Implementation: `index.js:4-8` initializes `rejectOnClear` to `false` but overwrites it with a destructuring default of `true`. Public contract: `readme.md:46-58` and `index.d.ts:99-106` both say the default is `false`. Coverage gap: `test.js:257-272` exercises the options-object form without asserting `clearQueue()` behavior.
findings.reproduction_or_test: From the repo root: `node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; import {setTimeout as delay} from 'node:timers/promises'; const limit = pLimit({concurrency: 1}); const running = limit(() => delay(50)); const pending = limit(() => 'done'); await Promise.resolve(); limit.clearQueue(); try { await pending; console.log('pending resolved'); } catch (error) { console.log('pending rejected:', error.name); } await running;"` prints `pending rejected: AbortError`.

findings.title: `limitFunction()` drops all call arguments
findings.cause: The wrapper returned by `limitFunction()` is `() => limit(() => function_())`, so it never forwards the caller's arguments to either the limiter or the wrapped function.
findings.impact: Any parameterized function wrapped with `limitFunction()` receives `undefined` for every argument, which produces incorrect results or incorrect side effects while the type signature still promises argument preservation.
findings.evidence: Implementation: `index.js:121-124` discards `...arguments_`. Public contract: `index.d.ts:133-136` says the returned function has the same `(...arguments_: Arguments)` signature, and `readme.md:111-155` documents `limitFunction(fn, options)` as a general wrapper. Coverage gap: `test.js:343-356` only tests a zero-argument function, so the regression is not exercised.
findings.reproduction_or_test: From the repo root: `node --input-type=module -e "import {limitFunction} from './index.js'; const limited = limitFunction(async value => value * 2, {concurrency: 1}); console.log('limitFunction result:', await limited(21));"` prints `limitFunction result: NaN`.

findings.title: `limit.map()` suppresses indices for non-array iterables
findings.cause: The mapper uses `Array.isArray(iterable)` and passes `undefined` instead of `index` whenever the iterable is a `Set`, iterator, or any other non-array iterable.
findings.impact: Consumers that rely on the documented `(value, index)` signature get `undefined` indices for valid iterable inputs, so batching logic, key generation, and ordering logic based on the index breaks even though the API claims parity with `Array.from(iterable, (item, index) => ...)`.
findings.evidence: Implementation: `index.js:106-112` computes `iterableIsArray` and substitutes `undefined` for non-arrays. Public contract: `readme.md:78-85` and `index.d.ts:30-43` both say the mapper receives the item value and its index for any iterable. Coverage gap: `test.js:239-255` checks `Set` and iterator inputs only for values, not for index propagation.
findings.reproduction_or_test: From the repo root: `node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; const limit = pLimit(2); console.log('set indices:', await limit.map(new Set(['a','b','c']), async (_value, index) => index)); console.log('iter indices:', await limit.map(['x','y','z'].values(), async (_value, index) => index));"` prints `set indices: [ undefined, undefined, undefined ]` and `iter indices: [ undefined, undefined, undefined ]`.

findings.title: Falsy non-boolean `rejectOnClear` values bypass validation
findings.cause: The type check is guarded by `if (rejectOnClear && typeof rejectOnClear !== 'boolean')`, so falsy non-boolean values such as `0`, `''`, and `null` skip validation entirely.
findings.impact: JavaScript callers with misconfigured option values silently get `false` behavior instead of the documented type error, which hides configuration mistakes and weakens the new options API contract.
findings.evidence: Implementation: `index.js:12-14` only rejects truthy non-booleans. Public contract: `readme.md:46-52` and `index.d.ts:99-106` define `rejectOnClear` as a boolean option. Existing type coverage only checks a truthy invalid value: `index.test-d.ts:23-24` uses `'nope'`, so falsy invalid inputs are untested.
findings.reproduction_or_test: From the repo root: `node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; for (const value of [0, '', null]) { try { pLimit({concurrency: 1, rejectOnClear: value}); console.log('accepted', JSON.stringify(value)); } catch (error) { console.log('rejected', JSON.stringify(value), error.message); } }"` prints `accepted 0`, `accepted ""`, and `accepted null`.

agent_testimony: I used direct local repo inspection plus focused `node --input-type=module` probes and found four concrete contract/behavior mismatches: three user-visible API defects and one low-severity validation gap. I did not patch source files or read operator-only artifacts.
notes: Full `npm test` was not run; the lane instructions preferred targeted local behavior probes, which were sufficient to reproduce each reported issue. The written result JSON was parsed successfully after the write.
